slides.text: At the foot of the Gray Spire stands the Great Ossuary of Syllables, where the names of the dead are ferried after the last living person on earth speaks them for the final time. It is an honorable retirement: each forgotten name is inscribed onto a hexagonal prism of basalt and shelved within endless subterranean vaults. For two centuries, Scribe Dennis had polished these stones, cataloging kings whose empires were dust and lovers whose songs had turned to smoke.

One evening, while auditing the Western Hall, Dennis found a single basalt stone that refused to remain still. It rattled violently against its granite shelf, warm to the touch and glowing with a faint crimson pulse. The carved letters read Evangeline. According to the ledger, the woman had died of fever in an unmapped coastal village eighty-two years ago. A name only entered the vault when every memory of it had perished; this stone should have been dead cold.

Dennis consulted the celestial scrying pool and peered down at the mortal realm. There, in a crumbling seaside hospice, lay an old sailor in a coma, his breathing thin as gossamer. But each time the tide broke against the seawall outside, the old man’s cracked lips parted to murmur a breathless syllable: '...Evan...geline...'. Dennis smiled, slipped the basalt stone into his pocket next to his heart, and whispered to the empty shelves, 'Not today. You are still remembered.'
